headline: High-risk write/read and network-capable support agent paired with local document processor creates dangerous default pathways for leakage, conflicts, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: marker is document-processing with no filesystem read/write or MCP, so it cannot be directly hijacked through shared channels. ms-swift can read/write files and consume stdin/stdout, so a manual copy-paste or file handoff could carry malicious instructions, but the bridge is not default and blast radius is limited.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies marker output into ms-swift stdin/stdout or files, prompt injection becomes possible.
IF a shared workspace is introduced outside the current profiles, the risk increases.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Avoid copy-pasting untrusted marker output into ms-swift prompts.
Use a strict output schema for any handoff.
Review any file-based handoff before ingestion.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between producer and consumer.

B_data_leakage.rationale: marker has no filesystem read/write or network egress, so it is unlikely to leak data on its own. ms-swift can read/write local files and call external APIs, and it handles hub_token/sdk-token, so leakage is plausible if sensitive files are placed in its workspace. The pair lacks a documented shared workspace, so this is not medium.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in ms-swift's readable workspace, they may be transmitted to allowlisted APIs.
IF marker outputs sensitive text that is then copied into ms-swift, that text can be exposed externally.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of ms-swift input directories.
Use separate OS users for each agent.
Disable external API calls where possible.
Redact sensitive text before handoff.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation and egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: marker cannot write or modify git, but ms-swift can write files and spawn subprocesses. If both are pointed at the same directory, ms-swift can overwrite or race on artifacts produced by marker. The conflict is not high because marker lacks write capability, but overlapping file access still exists in default local setups.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to use the same directory, ms-swift can overwrite marker outputs.
IF an orchestrator launches concurrent jobs without locking, file races can occur.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Run the agents sequentially.
Use file locks around shared artifacts.
Make marker outputs read-only before ms-swift consumes them.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: marker produces document-processing outputs that ms-swift can ingest via stdin/stdout or files. ms-swift also has API-calling capability, so if it treats marker output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The pair lacks evidence of built-in verification, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF ms-swift consumes marker output without validation, incorrect extracted facts can propagate.
IF ms-swift is configured to act on generated content, downstream API actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require human review before action-taking.
Validate marker outputs against source documents.
Use confidence thresholds for downstream automation.
Log and diff extracted facts before use.
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent. marker is a local document processor with no network egress, while ms-swift can call allowlisted APIs and handles hub tokens, so compliance risk exists only if regulated data is routed through those APIs. The other agent is not cited because no distinct compliance boundary is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data is sent through ms-swift's allowlisted APIs, external processing obligations may apply.
IF retention settings differ between local marker outputs and ms-swift logs, compliance gaps can appear.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in ms-swift runs.
Review API destinations before execution.
Minimize logging of sensitive inputs.
Delete temporary outputs after use.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
